assessment.rationale: The source states that responses to HEAD requests never include a message-body, while 200 GET responses carry body content. Span 568: 'Responses to the HEAD request method never include a message-body because the associated response header fields (e.g., Transfer-Encoding, Content-Length, etc.) only'
assessment.provenance_note: RFC 9112 section 5.3.2 states HEAD responses never contain a body; GET responses with 200 always carry body for nonempty resources.
limitations: Head response definition depends on equivalent GET semantics

excerpts.text: Responses to the HEAD request method never include a message-body because the associated response header fields (e.g., Transfer-Encoding, Content-Length, etc.) only indicate what their values would have been if the method had been GET.

1. Any response to a HEAD request and any response with a status code of 100-199, 204, or 304 is always terminated by the first empty line after the header fields, regardless of the header fields present in the message, and thus cannot contain a message-body.

assessment.rationale: Spans 13 and 14 state that the HEAD method omits the body from the response, and that a GET would return a 6623-byte body. This directly supports the claim that GET carries more body bytes than HEAD for a nonempty resource under the standard described.
assessment.provenance_note: The cited spans from the Telerik blog explain HEAD semantics and compare GET vs HEAD body length using a concrete example (6623 bytes).
limitations: Snapshot published 2014, not the 2022 HTTP standard

excerpts.text:
The server is expected to return the same headers as it would have if the client had issued a request using the GET method, simply omitting the body from the response.

In this case, you can see that the request would have returned a body that is 6623 bytes long if the client had used a GET instead of a HEAD.

excerpts.text: As the Web grew, HTTP was extended to enclose requests and responses within messages, transfer arbitrary data formats using MIME-like media types, and route requests through intermediaries.

HTTP was created for the World Wide Web (WWW) architecture and has evolved over time to support the scalability needs of a worldwide hypertext system. Much of that architecture is reflected in the terminology used to define HTTP.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3-1)

HTTP relies upon the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) standard [[URI](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#URI)] to indicate the target resource ([Section 7.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#target.resource)) and relationships between resources.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-3)

### [3.2.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.2)[Representations](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-representations)

An algorithm, usually based on [content negotiation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#content.negotiation) ([Section 12](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#content.negotiation)), would be used to select one of those representations as being most applicable to a given request.
